abstract: Macula densa (MD) cells are key sensory and regulatory cells in the kidney; however, they have been difficult to study because of a lack of cell-specific, user-friendly in vivo research tools. Here we demonstrate the high affinity of wild-type Adeno-Associated Virus serotype 9 (AAV9) for MD cells and the feasibility of AAV9-mediated MD cell-specific genetic manipulations when administered to neonatal mice or after a temporary physiological challenge (low-salt diet) in the adult. A single intraperitoneal injection of low-dose AAV9-GFP given to neonatal mice on postnatal days P2-3 resulted in highly MD-specific and efficient transduction (~85% of all GFP+ cells were Nos1+ MD cells). Proof-of-concept studies used AAV9 to overexpress or knock down biologically relevant genes in MD cells and establish MD gain- and loss-of-function (Gof/Lof) mouse models for initial functional and structural phenotyping using intravital multiphoton microscopy at the single-nephron level and immunofluorescence-based histological analysis. RNAscope confirmed the MD-specific knockdown of Pregnancy-associated plasma protein A2 (Pappa2) expression by AAV9-Pappa2 shRNA treatment in MD-Pappa2Lof mice, and the MD-specific overexpression of Cell communication network 1 (Ccn1) by AAV9-Ccn1 mRNA treatment in MD-Ccn1Gof mice. The mouse phenotypes revealed alterations in classic MD/juxtaglomerular functions (renin control and tubuloglomerular feedback-mediated glomerular hemodynamics) as well as in newly emerging MD cell functions (tissue remodeling). MD-specific genetic manipulations in vivo via AAV9-mediated gene delivery may enable future studies of MD cell functions, including the MD program for endogenous kidney tissue remodeling and regeneration, and support the development of MD cell-targeting gene therapies for kidney diseases.
